title: God Promises David a Lasting Family
overview: David wants to build a temple for God, but God instead promises to build David a royal family line that will last forever.

parts.label: David's plan for a temple (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: With his wars on pause, David notices he lives in a fine palace of cedar, a costly imported wood, while the ark, the sacred chest that stood for God's presence, still sits in a tent. Nathan the prophet assumes such a good idea must please God and tells him to go ahead.

parts.label: God says not you (vv. 4-7)
parts.note: That same night God corrects Nathan, pointing out that he has traveled with Israel in a tent since Egypt and never asked any leader for a grand building. The point seems to be that God's presence never depended on a building, and the plan was David's idea, not God's request.

parts.label: What God has already done (vv. 8-11a)
parts.note: God reminds David that he began as a shepherd and that every victory came from God, not the other way around. God promises David a great name and a settled, safe home for the people.

parts.label: God will build David a house (vv. 11b-13)
parts.note: David wanted to build God a house, meaning a temple, but God turns the word around and promises to build David a house, meaning a line of kings. David's son, usually understood as Solomon, will be the one to build the temple.

parts.label: A son and a lasting throne (vv. 14-16)
parts.note: God will treat this king like a son, punishing his wrongs through human hands, but never withdrawing his faithful love as he did from Saul, the king before David. Christians later read this promise of a throne that lasts forever as pointing to Jesus, who is called a descendant of David.

parts.label: David's amazed prayer (vv. 17-29)
parts.note: David sits before the LORD and asks who he is that God should promise so much to his family. He praises God for choosing and rescuing Israel, then asks God simply to do what he has promised.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the 'forever' promise was first meant only for Solomon and David's royal line, and was later applied to Jesus, or whether it was a prophecy about a coming messianic king from the start.
think: Is it harder for you to accept something good you did not earn than to give something you chose to give, and why might that be?
